Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 36, verse 8–12:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, We have put shackles around their necks﴾, concerning which there are three opinions:

The first: it is a parable which Allah Most High struck for them regarding their refusal of guidance, like the refusal of one who is shackled to act freely. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The second: what al-Suddi related, that some men of Quraysh conspired against the Prophet ﷺ and came intending that, so their hands were brought up to their necks, and they could not extend a hand toward him.

The third: that what is meant is that Allah, glorified is He, made for them in the Fire shackles upon their necks, and the word "ja'l" (making) here is taken from "ju'alah" (wage), which is the reward, as if their wage in the Fire is the shackles. This was related by Ibn Bahr.

Concerning His saying: ﴿around their necks﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: it means around their hands, so necks is used as a metonym for hands, since the shackle is on the hands. This was said by al-Kalbi, and Qutrub related that in the recitation of Ibn Abbas it is: (Indeed, We have put shackles around their right hands).

The second: that it literally means around the necks, because the hands are gathered with the neck in the shackle. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

﴿So they are up to the chins﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

The first: up to the faces, so the chins are used as a metonym for them, since they are part of them. This was said by Qatadah, meaning his hand is shackled at his face.

The second: that they are the chins which hang below the lip at the bottom of the face, because their hands touch them when they are raised.

﴿So they are with heads raised high﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations:

The first: raising their heads and placing their hands over their mouths. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it is one who lifts his gaze toward the place where his foot treads. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: it is lowering the gaze while raising the head, taken from the camel "muqmah," which is one that raises its head and closes its eyelids in winter when it comes to foul water. Al-Naqqash related this.

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And present to them a parable: the companions of the town, when the messengers came to it﴾. This town is Antioch (Antakiyya), according to the consensus of all the exegetes (mufassirun).

﴿When We sent to them two, and they denied them both﴾. The scholars differed concerning their names, in three opinions:

The first: they were Shim'un and Yuhanna, said by Shu'ayb.

The second: Sadiq and Sadduq, said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b al-Ahbar and Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The third: Sam'an and Yahya, related by al-Naqqash.

﴿Then We strengthened them with a third﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations:

The first: "then We reinforced," said by Mujahid.

The second: "then We added," said by Ibn Jurayj.

The third: "We strengthened," derived from 'izza, which is an impregnable strength; from it comes the saying: "Whoever is mighty (ʿazza) prevails (bazz)."

The scholars differed concerning his name, in two opinions:

One of them: Yunus, said by Shu'ayb.

The second: Shulum, said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b and Wahb.

The king of Antioch was one of the Pharaohs, and he worshipped idols along with its people. They had three idols which they worshipped; al-Naqqash mentioned that their names were Rumus, and it is said Warṭamis.

The scholars differed concerning the name of the king, in two opinions:

The words of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Follow those who ask no wage of you﴾ may bear two meanings:

One of them: that he said this as a pointer to their truthfulness.

The second: that he said this as an encouragement to respond to them.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And We made springs gush forth therein﴾ ﴿that they may eat of its fruit, and of what their hands have made﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: "mā" is affirmative, and its implied meaning is: "and of what their hands have made." This is the view of al-Kalbi, al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah.

The second interpretation: "mā" is negative (jaḥd), and on this view there are two possibilities:

One: "and of what their hands did not make," meaning the rivers which Allah, glorified is He, caused to flow for them.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: he means the Euphrates, the Tigris, the river of Balkh, and the Nile of Egypt.

The second: "and of what their hands did not make," meaning the crops which Allah the Exalted caused to grow for them.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: he means all the kinds, as stated by al-Suddi.

The second: he means from the palm trees, the trees and the crops, each kind of which is a pair.

﴿And from themselves﴾. In this there is evidence of the resemblance of animals to them in that each is a pair, male and female.

﴿And of what they do not know﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: he means the soul (rūḥ), which Allah knows and no one else knows.

The second: what is seen rarely of animals and plants.

It may also bear a third meaning: of what you do not know of the changing of the fetus in its mother's womb.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾, meaning: We draw forth from it the day, i.e. its light. It is derived from the skinning of a sheep (salkh al-shah) when it comes out of its hide.

﴿Then they are in darkness﴾, meaning: in gloom, because the light of the day mingles with the air and illuminates it; when it is withdrawn from it, it becomes dark.

﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

The first: meaning, until its affair comes to an end at the expiry of the world. This is related by Ibn ʿIsa.

Two: then there is no defence for them. Related by Shaybān from Qatadah.

﴿Nor are they rescued﴾ has two interpretations:

One: from drowning.

Two: from punishment.

﴿Except as a mercy from Us﴾ has two interpretations:

One: except Our mercy. Said by Yahya ibn Salam.

Two: except a blessing from Us. Said by Muqatil.

﴿And as enjoyment for a time﴾ has two interpretations:

One: until death. Said by Qatadah.

Two: until the Resurrection. Said by Yahya.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 36, verses 48–50:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you should be truthful?"﴾ Regarding this there are two views:

First: it refers to what they were promised of punishment. This was said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

Second: it refers to what they were promised of victory over them. This was said by Qatadah.

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿They await not but a single blast which will seize them﴾. Al-Suddi said: it is the first blast (al-nafkhah al-ula) of Israfil, which the last of this community among the polytheists awaits.

Nu'aym narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Hour will come while two men have spread out their garment, trading with it, and they will not fold it until the Hour comes. A man will lower his scale, and will not raise it until the Hour comes. A man will repair his water-trough to water his livestock, and will not water them until the Hour comes. A man will raise a morsel to his mouth, and it will not reach his mouth until the Hour comes."

﴿And they will be disputing﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

First: they will be speaking about their livelihoods and their trade. This was said by al-Suddi.

Second: they will be disputing over the repelling of the second creation (al-nash'ah al-thaniyah). This was related by Ibn Isa.

﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾, meaning: one of them will not be able to bequeath to another what he holds of rights.

It may also bear a second meaning: that they will not be able to enjoin one another to repentance and giving up (sin).

﴿Nor will they return to their families﴾, meaning: to their dwellings. Qatadah said: because they were hurried away from that.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 36, verses 51–54:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾ This is the second blast for the resurrection (al-nash'a), and it is said that between the two blasts there are forty years.

Al-Mubarak ibn Fudala narrated from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Between the two blasts there are forty: in the first, Allah, glory be to Him, causes every living thing to die by it, and in the last, Allah gives life by it to every dead thing."

The second blast is from the Hereafter.

Regarding the first there are two opinions:

One: that it is from this world; this was said by Ikrima.

The second: that it is from the Hereafter; this was said by al-Hasan.

﴿Then, behold, they will rush out from the graves (al-ajdath) to their Lord﴾ al-ajdath are the graves, the singular of which is jadath.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿yansiluna﴾ (they will rush out), there are three interpretations:

One: they will come out, said by Ibn Abbas and Qatada. The poet said:

So strip off my garments from your garments (fasulli thiyabi min thiyabiki tansali)

The second: they will hasten, like the saying of the poet:

The wolf's swift gait, when evening came near, the night cooled upon him, so he hastened (asalan al-dhi'bi amsa qariban ... barada al-layl alayhi fa-nasal)

The third: they will extricate themselves from the state of forgetfulness (al-sulu), said by Ibn Bahr.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿They will say: "Woe to us! Who has raised us up from our resting place?"﴾ Qatada said: This is the sleep between the two blasts, during which the punishment of the grave does not cease from them except in it.

Regarding the interpretation of this saying there are two opinions:

One: that it is the saying of the believers, and then they answer themselves, saying:

(p-24) ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth﴾; related by Ibn Isa.

The second: that it is the saying of the disbelievers, because of their denial of resurrection, and it is said to them: ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth.﴾

Regarding who says this to them there are two opinions:

One: that it is the saying of the believers to them when they rise from the graves with them; said by Qatada.

The second: that it is the saying of the angels to them; said by al-Hasan.

Regarding this there are two possibilities:

One: that it is an indication of the resting place in full, in accordance with His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿who has raised us up from this our resting place﴾, and on this basis the pause must be after it.

The second: that ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth﴾ is a new beginning, so that it refers to the promise, and the pause is before it and the beginning is from it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 36, verse 55–58:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busily occupied, enjoying themselves﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions:

The first: it refers to the deflowering of the virgins (ifdiḍāḍ al-abkār). This was said by al-Ḥasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Ibn Masʿūd and Qatādah.

The second: it refers to the striking of the lutes (ḍarb al-awtār). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās and Musāfiʿ ibn Abī Shurayḥ.

The third: it refers to bounty (niʿmah). This was said by Mujāhid.

The fourth: it refers to being occupied with what the people of the Fire suffer. This was said by Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid and Abān ibn Taghlib.

It is related with a ḍammah on the ghayn (shughul), and it is also read with a sukūn (shughl), and in the latter there are two possibilities:

One: that shughul with a ḍammah means "the beloved" (al-maḥbūb).

The second: shughl with a sukūn means "the occupation" (al-marwah, i.e. manliness or a matter of honour). On this reading, it is not permissible to read it with a sukūn regarding the people of the Garden, nor to read it with a ḍammah regarding the people of the Fire.

﴿Fākihūn﴾ is also read fakihūn, without an alif.

Regarding the difference between the two readings there are two possibilities:

One: they are the same in meaning, and both mean the same thing, as one says fākih and fakih, just as one says ḥādhir and ḥadhir. This was said by al-Farrāʾ.

The second: their meanings differ in the language. Fakih is one who jests about the faults of people, while fākih is one who possesses fruit (dhū al-fākihah). This was said by Abū ʿUbayd, who recited:

"Fakihun beside the table, when a northeasterly wind blows, uprooting the firmly-fixed tent-pegs."

Here there are four interpretations: One: joyful (faraḥūn), said by Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second: enjoying luxury (nāʿimūn), said by Qatādah.

The third: self-admiring (muʿjabūn), said by Mujāhid.

The fourth: possessors of fruit, as one says shāḥim lāḥim, meaning possessing fat and meat, and as the poet said:

"You deceived me and claimed that you ∗∗∗ are a dweller of milk in summer, a possessor of dates."

That is: possessing milk and dates.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿They and their spouses are in shade﴾. Concerning this there are two possibilities:

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 36, verses 59–62:

His statement, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And separate yourselves today, O you criminals.﴾ On this there are two interpretations:

The first: this was said by al-Kalbi, because the believers and the disbelievers are gathered together with their messengers, and therefore they are commanded to separate.

It may therefore carry two meanings:

The first: that the separation occurs at the standing (on the Day of Resurrection).

The second: at the turning back toward the Fire.

Dawud ibn al-Jarrah said: the Muslims separate from the criminals, except the person of desire (sahib al-hawa), who remains with the criminals.

His statement, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude (jibillan kathiran).﴾ On this there are three interpretations:

The first: large groups (juyuban kathiratan), said by Qatadah.

The second: many nations (umaman kathiratan), said by al-Kalbi.

The third: a great number of creation (khalqan kathiran), said by Mujahid and Mutarrif.

Al-Dahhak related that a single jibil is ten thousand, and that "kathir" is what none can count except Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 36, verse 63–67:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿Today We shall seal their mouths﴾ has two aspects:

The first: that what prevents them from speaking is the sealing upon them.

The second: that it is a seal placed upon them, so that they see but are prevented from speaking.

Regarding the cause of the sealing there are four aspects:

The first: because they said, ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾, so God sealed their mouths until their limbs spoke. This was said by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.

The second: so that the people of the place of standing may recognise them and distinguish them from others. This was said by Ibn Ziyad.

The third: because the testimony of one who does not speak is more binding than the testimony of one who speaks, since it comes out as a sign of miracle, although it is a day on which there is no need for miracles.

The fourth: so that it is known that his limbs, which were helpers to them in what concerned their own selves, have become witnesses against them concerning their Lord.

(p-28) ﴿And their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn﴾. Regarding their speech there are three opinions:

The first: that a mark appears upon them which takes the place of their speech, as the poet said:

"The two eyes have said, 'We hear and obey,' and their tears, like pearls not yet pierced, have fallen."

The second: that those appointed over them bear witness against them.

The third: that God creates in them that by which speech becomes possible from them.

al-Sha'bi narrated from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It will be said to his members, 'Speak!' and they will speak of his deeds. Then he will be left between himself and speech, and he will say: 'Away with you and far off, it was for your sake that I was disputing.'"

If it is asked: why did He say, ﴿And their hands will speak to Us and their feet will bear witness﴾, making what came from the hand speech and what came from the foot testimony?

It is said: because the hand is directly engaged in his deed, while the foot is present; the statement of one present about another is testimony, and the statement of the doer about himself is a confession. Therefore he expressed what proceeded from the hands by speech, and what proceeded from the feet by testimony.

Shurayh ibn Ubayd narrated from Uqbah ibn Amir, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "The first bone of a person to speak on the day the mouths are sealed is his left thigh from the leg."

It is possible that the thigh's precedence in speech over the other limbs is because he perceives the pleasure of his disobediences through his senses, which are in the upper part of his body, and the closest limbs of the lower part to them is the thigh; so it was fitting, due to its nearness to them, that it should precede in testimony against them. The left was given precedence because desire is stronger in the right-hand parts of the limbs than in the left-hand parts, so the left precedes the right because its desire is weaker.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes, so they would race for the path﴾ has two aspects:

The first: We would have blinded the eyes of the polytheists in this world, so they would go astray from the way and not see, as a punishment for them. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: We would have blinded their hearts, so they would go astray from the truth and not be guided to it. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

al-Akhfash and Ibn Qutaybah said: the one who is "maṭmus" is the one who has no slit between his eyelids, derived from the wind obliterating a trace (ṭams).

﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾ has three interpretations:

The first: We would have made them sit upon their feet. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: We would have destroyed them in their dwellings. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: We would have changed their creation so that they could not go back. This was said by al-Suddi.

﴿So they would not be able to proceed, nor would they return﴾ has two aspects:

The first: if We had done that to them, they would not be able to advance or hold back. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: they would not be able to proceed in this world, nor return in it. This was said by Abu Salih.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 36, verses 71–73:**

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, from what Our hands have done, cattle?﴾ On this there are two views:

The first: it means by Our power. This was said by al-Hasan (al-Basri), as in His saying ﴿And the heaven We built with hands﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 47], meaning with power.

The second: it means from Our action and Our making, without Our entrusting it to anyone other than Us. This was said by al-Suddi.

Al-an'am (cattle): camels, cows and sheep.

﴿So they are for them owners﴾. On this there are three views:

The first: they are controllers (dabitun), said by Qatada, and from it is the saying of the poet:

؎ I have become one who no longer carries a weapon, nor controls the halter of a camel when it bolts.

The second: they are those who have mastery (mutbiqun), narrated by Ma'mar.

The third: they are those who possess them (muqtanun), which is the meaning of the saying of Ibn 'Isa.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And We have subjected them to them﴾. On this there are three views:

The first: We made them good for them (wa tayyabna-ha), said by Ibn 'Isa.

The second: We made them subservient to them (sakhkharna-ha), said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: We made them possessors of them (mallakna-ha).

﴿So from them is their riding﴾. Al-rukub, with a ḍamma, is the verbal noun of rakiba yarkabu rukuban (to ride). Al-rakub, with a fatha, is the animal that is fit to be ridden.

﴿And from them they eat﴾, meaning the flesh of what is eaten from them.

﴿And for them in them are benefits﴾. Qatada said: these are the wearing of their wool.

﴿And drinks﴾, meaning drinking their milk. ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾, meaning to the Lord of this blessing, by affirming His oneness and obeying Him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they are an army [jund] for them, brought forth [muhdarun]﴾. He means that the polytheists have an army for their idols. Regarding the word jund (army) here, there are two interpretations:

The second: helpers (a'wan).

The third: they will be brought forth to defend them and to prevent harm from them. This was said by Humayd.

Qatadah said: they will be angry for their gods, while their gods will not help them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 36, verse 74–76:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they are an army [jund] for them, brought forth [muhdarun]﴾. He means that the polytheists have an army for their idols. Regarding the word jund (army) here, there are two interpretations:

One of them: a faction (shi'ah). This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

The second: helpers (a'wan).

Regarding ﴿muhdarun﴾ (brought forth), there are three interpretations:

One of them: they will be brought forth at the reckoning (al-hisab). This was said by Mujahid.

The second: they will be brought forth into the Fire. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: they will be brought forth to defend them and to prevent harm from them. This was said by Humayd.

Qatadah said: they will be angry for their gods, while their gods will not help them.

Second: it was revealed concerning al-As ibn Wa'il, who took a bone from the gravel and crumbled it in his hand, then said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Will Allah bring this back to life after it has decayed?" This was said by Ibn Abbas.

﴿Then at once he becomes a open adversary﴾: that is, he becomes a disputant in contention, clearly presenting his argument. By this he means that he became, after having been nothing, an open adversary. This may carry two meanings:

First: that He alerts him by this to His blessings upon him.

Second: that He points him by this to the bringing of the dead back to life, just as He originated him after he had been nothing.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And he sets forth for Us a parable and forgets his own creation﴾, refers to the one we have already mentioned, and it may bear two meanings:

First: that is, he left aside his own creation, failing to take it as evidence.

Second: he was heedless of taking a lesson from it.

﴿Say: "He will give them life who originated them the first time"﴾: that is, whoever was able to bring them into being the first time from nothing is able to restore them in the second creation from something.

﴿And He is Knowing of every creation﴾: that is, [He knows] how He originates and how He restores.

This may bear two meanings from Him:

First: that Allah, exalted is He, alerts by this to His power, which nothing can overcome.

Second: that He points by it to the bringing of the dead to life, just as fire is kindled by ignition.

Al-Kalbi said: fire can be struck from every tree except the jujube (al-unnab).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 36, verse 81–83:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Indeed, His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ In this there are two views:

The first: its meaning is that He commands and it comes into existence.

The second: what Qatadah said, that there is nothing lighter in speech than ﴿Be﴾ (kun), nor easier on the tongue of the Arabs than that. So Allah the Exalted made it a parable for His command in speed.

﴿So exalted is He in whose hand is the dominion (malakut) of all things﴾ In this there are two views:

The first: the treasuries of all things.

The second: the sovereignty of all things, though there is in it an emphasis (mubalaghah).

(p-35) ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾, meaning on the Day of Resurrection, when He will reward the doer of good and punish the doer of evil.

Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, every thing has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin. Whoever recites it on a night will be given the ease of that night, and whoever recites it on a day will be given the ease of that day. And indeed, the people of Paradise will have the Qur'an lifted from them, so they will recite nothing from it except Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin."
